Modal split of inland passenger transport in the EU

Eurostat tran_hv_psmod

Author

Mohd Zamin Quadri

Published

October 19, 2026

What this is

A worked example of reading an official statistical API in R and reporting what it says, with every number in the prose computed from the data rather than typed in.

The dataset is Eurostat’s modal split of inland passenger transport: for each country and year, the share of inland passenger-kilometres travelled by passenger car, by train, and by motor coach, bus or trolley bus. The three shares sum to 100% by construction, so this measures how people travel rather than how much.

The raw response is committed at data/raw/tran_hv_psmod.json with its SHA-256 and retrieval date in data/raw/PROVENANCE.md, so the report renders offline and the figures cannot drift from the numbers underneath them.

The snapshot covers 35 countries and the years 1990 to 2024, though coverage is uneven: not every country reports every year, and the series are sparse rather than rectangular.

How complete is the data?

Worth establishing before drawing any trend, because a line chart over a sparse series invites the reader to interpolate through years nobody measured.

Code 
cars <- countries[countries$vehicle == "CAR", ]

# as.data.frame(table(...)) makes `year` a factor whatever stringsAsFactors
# says, and as.integer() on a factor returns the level index rather than the
# label. Going via as.character() is what keeps these actual years.
per_year <- as.data.frame(table(year = cars$year), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
per_year$year <- as.integer(as.character(per_year$year))
names(per_year)[2] <- "n_countries"

ggplot(per_year, aes(x = year, y = n_countries)) +
  geom_col(fill = MODE_COLOURS[["Passenger cars"]], width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1990, 2025, 5)) +
  labs(
    title = "Countries reporting a car share, by year",
    subtitle = "Coverage thins out at both ends of the series",
    x = NULL, y = "Countries reporting",
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report()

Coverage peaks at 35 countries in 2010. The most recent year with at least 90% of that peak is 2024, which is the year used below wherever a single-year comparison is made. Picking the latest year present instead would compare a handful of early reporters against each other.

The long-run picture

Code 
eu <- modal[modal$geo == "EU27_2020", ]

ggplot(eu, aes(x = year, y = value, colour = vehicle_label)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = MODE_COLOURS) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "The car's share of EU inland passenger travel has barely moved",
    subtitle = "Share of inland passenger-kilometres, EU27 (2020 definition)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report()

The car share stood at 82.0% in 2000 and 82.5% in 2024, a change of +0.5 percentage points across 24 years. Whatever has changed in European transport policy over that period, it has not changed what share of distance is driven.

Who depends on cars most?

Code 
ref <- cars[cars$year == latest_full, ]
ref <- ref[order(ref$value), ]
ref$geo_label <- factor(ref$geo_label, levels = ref$geo_label)

ggplot(ref, aes(x = value, y = geo_label)) +
  geom_col(
    aes(fill = geo == "DE"),
    width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#7A6BA8", "FALSE" = "#9DB8D2")) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", value)),
    hjust = -0.15, size = 3, colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100), labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Share of passenger-kilometres travelled by car, ", latest_full),
    subtitle = "Germany highlighted",
    x = NULL, y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_line())

In 2024 the range runs from 97.8% (Montenegro) down to 66.9% (Hungary), a spread of 30.9 percentage points. Germany sits at 84.1%, ranking 12 of 34.

Where rail actually gained

Code 
trains <- countries[countries$vehicle == "TRN", ]

# Each country's own first and last reported year, not a fixed window. A fixed
# window would drop every country whose series starts late, which is most of
# the 2004 and 2007 accession states.
change <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trains, trains$geo), function(g) {
  g <- g[order(g$year), ]
  if (nrow(g) < 2) return(NULL)
  data.frame(
    geo = g$geo[1],
    geo_label = g$geo_label[1],
    from_year = g$year[1],
    to_year = g$year[nrow(g)],
    change = g$value[nrow(g)] - g$value[1],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))

change <- change[order(change$change), ]
change$geo_label <- factor(change$geo_label, levels = change$geo_label)

ggplot(change, aes(x = change, y = geo_label, fill = change > 0)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#4E9A92", "FALSE" = "#C9A8A8")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in rail's share of passenger travel",
    subtitle = "Each country between its own first and last reported year, so the windows differ",
    x = "Percentage point change", y = NULL,
    caption = EUROSTAT_CAPTION
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_line())

14 of 32 countries increased rail’s share and 18 reduced it. The largest gain is Switzerland, up 7.3 percentage points between 1990 and 2024.

Each bar covers a different span of years, which is stated on the chart rather than hidden: a country reporting only since 2010 is not comparable with one reporting since 1990, and forcing a common window would have discarded most of the newer member states entirely.

What this does not show

  • Shares, not volumes. A falling car share is consistent with more driving, if rail grew faster. Nothing here measures total distance travelled.
  • Inland transport only. Air and sea are excluded by the dataset’s own definition, so this is not a complete picture of how people travel between countries.
  • Unequal windows. Countries enter the series at different dates. Every comparison above either uses a single stated year or labels the span it covers.
  • No causal claim. The report describes what the series contains. It does not attribute any change to any policy.
